Here are two ways to polish your text, depending on the format you prefer. 

Because the original piece carries deep literary, visceral, and emotional qualities, "professional" in this context translates to a **refined, publication-ready literary style** (such as a narrative essay or a polished contemporary poem).

---

### Option 1: Elevated Literary Prose (Best for essays, memoirs, or stories)

> There lies a distinct magic in decay—a quiet choreography reserved for the rotting, for the maggot-strewn piles of flesh accumulating upon the dung-ridden earth, and for the gathering damp that rusts and defiles. A trace of this lingers even within the most zoetic soul: a dancing child, arms flailing to an old ska song, inadvertently conducting day-old flies toward whatever rank refuge lies nearest. 
>
> Just today, as I walked along the river with my daughter riding in my backpack, I opened an email on my phone. Duffie had sent me a poem titled “Compost.” I began reading it aloud to my little girl, but before I could explain three words, Selma cried out, “Daddy, Daddy, snake!” 
>
> There in our path lay a snake, belly-up and still nerve-twitching—the lingering casualty of a passing bicycle or horse. “Pretty,” Selma said. “Yes,” I replied. Yet beneath my quiet assent echoed another—a acceptance of my own body, just beginning to show the subtle slack of age, and a deeper longing, a grasping in the dark for affirming flesh that whispers back: *Yes, yes, let us rot together, but not until we have drained whatever sap remains in these trees.*
>
> By morning, I awake to the memory of the coroner calling to ask the color of my father’s eyes. “Why?” I had asked. “Why can’t you simply look?” To which the coroner replied, with detached matter-of-factness: “Decay.”
>
> “Do you want some eggs, my love? I have a new way of preparing them. And look—look outside. I think this weather has a chance of holding.”

---

### Option 2: Refined Free-Verse Poetry (Best for contemporary poetic publication)

> There is magic in decay—  
> a dance performed  
> for the rotting, the maggot-strewn  
> piles of flesh accumulating  
> upon the dung-ridden earth,  
> and the damp that gathers, rusts, and defiles.  
> 
> A bit of this abides  
> in even the most zoetic soul:  
> a child’s flailing arms,  
> dancing to an old ska song,  
> conduct day-old flies away  
> to whichever rank refuge is near.  
> 
> Just today, walking by the river  
> with my daughter in my backpack,  
> I opened an email from Duffie—  
> a poem titled “Compost.”  
> I began reading it aloud to my little girl,  
> but barely three words in, Selma yelled:  
> *Daddy, Daddy, snake!*  
> 
> In the path lay a serpent,  
> belly up and nerve-twitching—  
> the ghost of some passing bicycle or horse.  
> *Pretty,* Selma said.  
> *Yes,* I answered.  
> 
> And beneath my *yes* lived another:  
> an affirmation to my own body,  
> just beginning to show signs of slack,  
> and another—my grasping in the dark  
> for affirming flesh that answers in turn:  
> *Yes, yes, let us rot together,  
> but not before we’ve drained  
> what sap remains in these trees.*  
> 
> I wake in the morning thinking of the coroner  
> calling to ask the color of my father’s eyes.  
> *Why?* I had asked. *Why can’t you just look?*  
> And the coroner, matter-of-factly, said:  
> *Decay.*  
> 
> Do you want some eggs, my love?  
> I have a new way of preparing them.  
> And look—look outside—  
> I think this weather has a chance of holding.

---

### Key Improvements Made:
* **Enhanced Cadence & Diction:** Smoothed out phrasing (e.g., changing *"whatever rank Native"* to *"whatever rank refuge"* for clarity and punchiness, while preserving terms like *"zoetic"*).
* **Improved Punctuation & Flow:** Added em-dashes and italics to heighten the dramatic shifts between imagery, internal monologue, and dialogue.
* **Preserved Every Detail:** All narrative elements (Duffie's email, Selma in the backpack, the dead snake, the coroner's phone call, the morning conversation over eggs) remain completely intact.

There is a captivating allure found within decomposition. A rhythmic process exists for decaying, maggot-infested piles of flesh resting on manure-covered soil, surrounded by the moisture that causes oxidation and contamination. A hint of this mortality resides even in the most energetic individuals. For instance, when a young child wildly swings her limbs while dancing to classic ska music, she swats away day-old flies, shooing them off toward whatever nearby foul area they originated from.

Earlier today, I was taking a stroll along the riverbank while carrying my daughter in a backpack carrier. I checked my smartphone's inbox and saw that an acquaintance named Duffie had emailed me a poem titled "Compost." I recited the piece to my little girl and began explaining it to her, but I barely spoke three words before Selma cut me off, yelling, "Daddy, Daddy, snake!" Positioned on the trail was a serpent lying upside down, its muscles still reflexively spasming—the lingering casualty of a recently passing bicycle or horse. Selma remarked that the creature was beautiful, and I agreed aloud. 

Yet, beneath my vocalized agreement was a deeper, unspoken consent: an acceptance of my own aging frame as it starts to show signs of sagging, and a silent reach in the dark for a comforting human touch. It is a mutual understanding that we will eventually rot together, but only after we have squeezed every last drop of life out of our remaining years. 

Upon waking the next morning, my mind recalls a conversation with the medical examiner, who phoned to ask about the shade of my late father's eyes. When I asked why he couldn't simply inspect them himself, the coroner bluntly answered that decomposition had set in. Shifting my focus back to the present, I affectionately ask my partner if she would like some eggs, explaining that I have discovered a new cooking method for them, and I urge her to look outdoors, noting that the pleasant weather might actually last.

Decay and mortality are not mere external forces that await us at the end of a long journey; they are universal, inescapable elements woven into the very fabric of our being. From the moment we enter the world, a quiet, imperceptible decline begins within every living soul. It is a shared inheritance, a silent architecture that underpins all life, reminding us that fragility is the price of existence.

This profound truth often reveals itself in the most unexpected moments. During a quiet afternoon walk along the river, a speaker and his young daughter stumbled upon a freshly injured snake resting at the water’s edge. Though the creature was slowly dying, its broken body quivering with remaining life, the young child did not recoil in horror. Instead, through the innocent lens of youth, she found it breathtaking, mesmerized by the brilliant, iridescent sheen of its scales catching the sunlight. In that fleeting encounter, the stark reality of death met the unshielded wonder of childhood, creating a quiet space for contemplation.

Observing the dying snake and his daughter’s reaction sparked a deep, internal shift within the speaker. Looking down at his own aging body—marked by the subtle passage of time—he felt a profound sense of acceptance. Rather than fighting the inevitable physical decline that awaits everyone, the encounter inspired a renewed commitment to the present. It fueled a quiet desire to live richly and intentionally alongside his partner, embracing the full spectrum of love and intimacy while they still possess the vitality to do so, fully aware that their bodies will one day yield to time.

Yet, the shadow of mortality is never easily dismissed, often anchored by memories that carry a sharper, colder weight. The speaker is drawn back to a poignant memory from his past: the death of his own father. He recalls the stark, unvarnished reality of that loss through the words of a coroner, who was unable to record the color of the father’s eyes because decay had already set in. This devastating detail serves as an unfiltered reminder of nature’s finality—a reminder that no amount of love or memory can preserve the physical vessel once life has departed.

Ultimately, the text navigates the delicate tension between the terrifying scale of loss and the persistent warmth of being alive. Despite the omnipresence of decay, the speaker does not surrender to despair. Instead, he grounds himself in the simple, sacred rituals of daily domestic life. It is within the warmth of the home, the laughter of a child, and the quiet companionship of a partner that the speaker finds solace. Hope, he discovers, is not found in the denial of death, but in the deliberate choice to cherish the beauty and light of the present moment.
outputs.L4:
We spend much of our lives engaged in a quiet conspiracy against time, carefully shielding ourselves from the relentless truth that our bodies are fragile, temporary vessels. We speak of growing old as if it were an unexpected turn of events rather than the explicit condition of our existence. Yet, try as we might to look away, the reality of physical decay continually breaks through our illusions, demanding to be seen. 

I was reminded of this fundamental truth on an ordinary Tuesday afternoon, coming upon a dying snake beside a gravel path. It was a creature designed for fluid power, yet there it lay, struck by a car or simply worn out by the elements, its glittering scales dulling under the harsh midday sun. Its movements were no longer light and lethal, but slow, agonizing spasms—a desperate, involuntary fight against the inevitable. Watching the life ebb out of its lithe frame was a visceral, unsettling mirror. It was nature stripped of all poetry: raw, unfeeling, and indifferent. Here was the physical world in its most honest state, reducing muscle and beauty to still, decaying matter.

That dying serpent pulled a shadow out of my past, echoing an older, deeper wound: the memory of my father’s final days. He had been a man of immense physical presence, a towering figure whose strength once seemed like an immovable law of my universe. To watch him recede into the white sheets of a hospital bed—his skin growing papery, his breathing ragged, his powerful hands rendered trembling and weak—was to watch the foundation of my childhood crumble. In his passing, mortality ceased to be an abstract concept debated by philosophers; it became a tangible inheritance. I saw my own future etched into the fading contours of his face and realized that I, too, was standing in the same slow-moving line.

Later that evening, returning home with these heavy thoughts clinging to me, I watched my young daughter running in the garden. She was a vision of untamed vitality, her cheeks flushed with heat, her laughter unburdened by any knowledge of time’s cruelty. As she tripped and ran into my arms, pressing her small, soft face against my shoulder, a sudden, sharp ache pierced my heart. I looked at her smooth skin and bright, clear eyes, overwhelmed by the realization that she, too, is bound to this earthbound cycle. The very body that now leaps so effortlessly will one day tire, fade, and yield to the same dark silence that claimed my father and the creature on the road.

Yet, in that fleeting moment of grief for a future not yet arrived, something shifted within me. The dread did not vanish, but it transformed. To stare directly into the abyss of our physical decline is not an invitation to despair; it is a call to awakening. Recognizing that our flesh is temporary does not diminish the beauty of our existence—it amplifies it.

If our bodies were permanent, if our time were infinite, no single breath or touch would carry any real weight. It is precisely because the snake dies, because my father passed, and because my daughter will grow old, that this moment right now burns with such desperate brilliance. Confronting our inescapable impermanence breaks down the walls of our indifference. It forces us to hold one another a little tighter, to forgive a little faster, and to look into the eyes of those we love with a profound, terrifying tenderness. 

In the end, embracing our decay is the ultimate act of living. We are fragile, yes, and we are passing away. But while we are here, trapped in these fading frames, we possess the extraordinary ability to love fully, to feel deeply, and to cherish every fleeting second of this fragile, beautiful life.

**The Quiet Horizon**

**The** world often moves at a relentless pace, demanding our constant attention and energy. In the rush of daily routines and endless notifications, it is easy to forget the simple beauty that surrounds us every single day.

Imagine standing on a quiet hilltop as the morning begins to break. Over **there**, past the gentle curves of the sleeping trees, a faint golden glow starts to spread across the sky, painting the clouds in shades of rose and amber. The cool breeze carries the scent of damp earth, whispering promises of a brand-new start. 

In moments like this, time seems to lose its grip. You do not need a grand plan or a complicated purpose to appreciate where you are; you **just** need to pause, breathe, and exist in the present moment. Nature quietly reminds us that peace isn't something we have to search endlessly for—sometimes, it is already waiting for us to notice it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary free verse poem that opens with the line "There is magic in decay." Connect themes of bodily aging, parenthood, mortality, and domestic love.
counterfactuals.output:
There is magic in decay.
Look at the kitchen table, its pine heart softened
by a decade of salt and spilled milk,
ringed with the pale moons of hot coffee mugs.
Nothing stays sharp here, and thank God.

The house settles, its floorboards groaning
in the same low register as your hips
when you rise from the rug.
I watch the silver invade your hair,
a quiet winter settling on the person I chose,
while my own hands grow mapped with violet veins—
skin turned to parchment that remembers every touch.

In the hallway, the pencil marks on the doorframe
climb like ivy.
Our daughter leaves her milk teeth in a velvet box;
she is shedding her smallness,
borrowing our height, filling the house
with a loud, bright weather.
Every inch she gains is an inch we yield.
We are giving up our smooth brows, our easy mornings,
composting our youth so her roots can run deep.

And at night, in the dim warmth of our bed,
when the rooms are finally quiet and the day’s dust settles,
I fit the bend of my knees into the bend of yours.
We creak like old timber.
We smell of tea, worn cotton, and the late hour.

To love you through the wear
is to know that light enters best
where the grain has begun to split—
that one day we will be nothing more than dust,
but tonight we are the sweet, rich earth
holding up the roof.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you draft a visceral, reflective poem about a father walking along a river with his toddler in a backpack, reflecting on aging, receiving an email about a poem called "Compost," seeing a dying snake, and remembering a call from a coroner about his father's passing?
counterfactuals.output:
The aluminum frame of the pack bites my hips,
a tight harness binding your heat to my spine.
Two years old, riding high on my shoulders,
your sweet, sour breath puffs against my ear—
a mix of swallowed milk and crushed clover.
Below us, the river grinds its grey belly against the rocks,
eating the bank, taking what it wants, moving on.

My knees give a dry, wet pop on the descent. 
Thirty-six years of cartilage ground down to dust;
I feel the slow, silent rust taking hold of my hinges.
Then the trail stops us. 

A garter snake, split by an owl’s talon or a careless boot,
writhes in a slow, agony-slurred ribbon on the mud.
Its dark scales are dulling, losing the sheen of the river,
its underbelly exposed—pale, translucent, twitching.
A heart beating outside the bone, refusing to stop.
You point a fat finger and babble a soft, meaningless word,
unaware of how hard a thing has to work just to die.

In my hip pocket, the phone buzzes once. A ghostly itch.
Earlier, squinting at the screen in the trailhead shade,
I’d opened an email about a draft called *Compost*—
a poem sent by a friend, full of rich loam, damp leaves,
the quiet, greedy way the earth swallows its own dead 
and turns them into sweet, blinding green.

Standing over the snake, watching its tongue flick at the empty air,
the cold memory opens in my chest like a trap door:
The coroner’s voice on the line, six autumns ago.
Flat. Efficient. A man who dealt in weights and measures.
*Your father,* he said, the words heavy and cold as lead sinkers,
*was found this morning. The air conditioning was off.*
No poetry in that room. Just the hard science of decay,
the way a man unspools when no one is watching,
leaving behind a smell that stays in the throat for weeks.

Now, you kick your little heels against my ribs,
demanding water, demanding motion, demanding the world.
You are so light, yet my shoulders ache with the future.
My father is in the soil now, broken down, consumed,
pushed into the roots of some nameless oak.
This snake will be ants and rot by nightfall. 

And I am the bridge between the ash and the sprout,
the middle man, carrying the living over the dead.
I shift the pack, feeling the heavy pull of gravity in my heels,
step carefully over the twitching tail,
and keep walking along the river,
where the water keeps tearing the earth away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem exploring the idea that even the most vibrant living things contain decay, blending imagery of rotting flesh, mundane family life, morbid memories of loss, and an intimate morning conversation over breakfast.
counterfactuals.output:
The sun cuts warm across the yellowed formica,
bleaching the salt shakers, lighting the dust.
You pass the jar of damson jam;
its dark, bruised paste holds tiny seeds like teeth.
Coffee steams between your sleepy palms,
a black, bitter wash from roasted, crushed things.

"Did you sleep well?" you ask, wiping butter from your lip.
Your thumb bears a small, pale flap of peeling skin—
a sliver of you already shed,
already dead, drifting silently onto the napkin.

I watch the pulse that thumps beneath your throat,
so quick and vibrant, a bird trapped in skin.
Yet under the soft bloom of your cheek,
I know the quiet arithmetic of flesh:
cells collapsing by the millions as we speak,
a sloughing away, an unspooling,
the secret rot that keeps the furnace warm.

It tastes like August twenty years ago—
the stray dog we found behind the tool shed,
her belly swollen, wet with iridescent flies,
a sweetness so thick it caught in the throat like honey.
Or my grandmother’s hospice bed,
her ankles graying, turned the color of bruised pears,
the room smelling faintly of copper and old urine
while we whispered that we loved her,
kissing the cold paper of her brow before the ice set in.

How strange that love requires a carcass.
You crack an egg against the skillet's edge;
the shell gives up its wet, clear belly,
the yellow eye bursting on the iron.
Beside the sink, the scrap-bucket hums—
yesterday’s melon rinds turning soft and grey,
a velvet fur of blue-green mold drinking the sugar,
turning life back into rich, black grease.

"You're quiet today," you say, reaching across the crumbs.
Your hand is warm, smelling of soap and morning salt.
I wrap my fingers around yours, feeling the narrow bones—
eight small stones in your wrist, waiting for the dirt,
brittle and perfect beneath the living meat.

"I’m just thinking," I say, leaning in to kiss your cheek,
breathing the sweet, warm decay of our breath,
"about how beautiful it is—
how everything we touch is slowly breaking down,
just to give us one more morning."
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: "There is magic in decay." Write a dark, narrative poem starting with this idea. Include a daughter named Selma, a dead snake on a path, thoughts on a decaying body, and end on a tender, everyday moment like making eggs.
counterfactuals.output:
There is magic in decay.
I spoke it low so Selma wouldn’t flinch,
stopping where the dirt path narrowed out
beneath the black oaks and the clinging briar.
Before us lay a snake, a heavy whip
unraveled on the sun-baked, dusty stone.
Three days dead, its copper skin had caved
like an old velvet sleeve left in the rain.

Selma crouched, her small knees silver-dusted,
her shadow pooling dark beside its nose.
A dozen iridescent beetles worked
its sunken jaw with sharp, industrious zeal,
turning scales to mica, wet flesh into soil.
She did not pull her hand away; she watched
the black flies weave their blue-green stitches through
the quiet ruin of its hollow spine.
"Is it broken?" she asked, her breathing slow.
"No," I whispered. "It is giving itself back."

My mind slid down into that cool, dark earth,
caught in the thought of my own future rot.
How soft it must be, when the work is done,
to feel the tight knot of the self unbind.
To lie in heavy shade while blood turns sweet,
while ribs give up their vigil over breath,
and marrow softens into damp, black grease.
The brain unspooling like a forgotten thread,
leaving no trace of fear, no grip on grief—
just skin yielding to mold, eyes turned to ferns,
a body finally learning how to rest.

Selma tugged my thumb. Her palm was hot.
"I’m hungry now," she said, and pulled me back
across the threshold of the afternoon.

We left the snake to its quiet, busy earth
and walked the track until the porch appeared,
stepping inside the shadow of our house.
I turned the gas, lit up the iron ring,
and fetched two pale brown eggs out from the bowl.
I struck the shells against the porcelain rim—
a sharp, clean snap—and let the yellow yolks
slump heavy in the pan of sizzling grease.
The whites bloomed wide and crisp around the edge.
Selma leaned close to watch the white foam rise,
holding her plate out with both hands, content,
as pepper fell like dust upon the gold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of modern conversational poetry about accepting mortality and the physical breakdown of the body through everyday encounters with nature, grief, and fatherhood.
counterfactuals.output:
My left knee makes a sound now—
a dry branch snapping under a heavy boot—
every time I squat down in the garden
to pull the bindweed out of the mint.
It doesn’t even hurt, not really.
It’s just a notice served by the foundation.
A quiet reminder that the house is settling.

Yesterday, my son asked why the white oak in the park
drops its thickest limbs in late August,
green leaves still clinging to the bark.
*Self-pruning,* I told him, trying to sound like a man
who understands the woods.
*It gets too heavy for its own heartwood. It lets go so it can stand.*

I didn’t tell him that my father used to say the exact same thing
about his own shoulder, right before he stopped lifting me,
right before his world shrank to the size of a recliner
and a window facing the bird feeder.
I just watched my boy run toward the swings,
his ankles made of light and rubber,
landing on the hard dirt like a cat,
while I negotiated the three porch steps
with the careful deliberation of an antique dealer
moving a glass vase.

He wants me to carry him up the hill.
He’s seven now, forty-five pounds of warm elbows and ambition.
When I hoist him onto my hip, I feel the lower disc shift—
a small pebble sliding down a creek bed.
He smells like sun-baked cotton and apple juice.
He presses his palm to my cheek and says,
*Daddy, your beard has gray hair in it today.*
Not *some* gray hair. Just *gray hair,*
as if it arrived all at once while he was sleeping.

And he’s right. The skin under my eyes is thin as tissue paper.
It doesn’t snap back the way it used to when I was twenty-five
and treated my body like a borrowed truck I didn't care to return.

We sit together on the damp bench near the woodline.
A line of black ants is busy dissecting a dead beetle,
carrying it piece by piece into the dark,
not with sadness, just with a quiet, terrifying efficiency.
The bench itself is rotting at the feet,
softened by ten winters of rain, moss blooming in the grain.

I used to think aging was a fight you lost.
A mugging in a dark alley.
But sitting here, watching the light slant yellow through the maples,
listening to my son breathe hard from running,
I think it’s closer to a trade.

My knees give out a little so he can leap higher.
My back stiffens so I am forced to sit still long enough
to actually notice the way the goldenrod leans into the wind.
My father left me his broad shoulders and his bad hips,
and now I am passing them down, slightly more worn,
to a boy who still thinks I am built of stone.

*Race you to the fence,* he shouts, already five yards ahead.

I don't even try to sprint.
I just walk behind him at a steady, clicking pace,
watching his small sneakers kick up clouds of dry dirt,
happy to be the one who is slowing down,
happy to let the shadow I cast
get a little longer in the afternoon sun.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
